chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskan, from Dawud ibn Farqad, Abu Yazeed, from Ibn Abu Shayba al-Zuhri, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Death, death! Indeed, death is inevitable. Death comes with what is in it; it comes with coolness, rest, and the blessed return to the High Paradise for the people of the Abode of Eternity, whose striving was for it and whose desire was in it. And Death comes with what is in it with misery, regret, and the losing return to the Blazing Fire for the people of the Abode of Deception, whose striving was for it and whose desire was in it.'

Then he said, and he (the Prophet) said: 'When the Guardianship of Allah and Happiness are deserved, the Term (of death) comes between the eyes, and Ambition goes behind the back. And when the Guardianship of Satan and Misfortune are deserved, Ambition comes between the eyes, and the Term goes behind the back.'

He said: And the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was asked, 'Which of the Believers is the most astute?' So he said: 'The one who remembers death the most, and the one who is most prepared for it.'
ai.seo_question: What distinguishes the death of the righteous from the wicked according to this hadith?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the dual nature of death as a transition point, contrasting the 'blessed return' for the righteous with the 'losing return' for the deceitful. It introduces a profound psychological insight: the righteous experience death as a visible reality while worldly hopes fade, whereas the wicked are distracted by fleeting ambitions until death strikes unexpectedly. This aligns with the Shia scholarly emphasis on *dhikr al-mawt* (remembrance of death) as the key metric for spiritual intelligence (*aklas*), urging believers to prioritize the eternal over the temporal.
